## Acknowledgements

The content and format of this guide is adapted from the Cornell Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Commercial Vegetable Production.

The guidelines in this bulletin reflect the current (and past) authors’ best effort to interpret a complex body of scientific research, and to translate this into practical management options. Following the guidance provided in this bulletin does not assure compliance with any applicable law, rule, regulation or standard, or the achievement of particular discharge levels from agricultural land.

Every effort has been made to provide correct, complete, and up-to-date pest management information for New York State at the time this publication was released (July 2026). Changes in pesticide registrations, regulations, and guidelines occurring after publication are available in county Cornell Cooperative Extension offices or from the Cornell IPM Pesticide Safety Education Program (PSEP) ([psep.cce.cornell.edu](https://psep.cce.cornell.edu/)).

Trade names used herein are for convenience only. No endorsement of products is intended, nor is criticism of unnamed products implied.

**This guide is not a substitute for pesticide labeling. Always read the product label before applying any pesticide.**

## A note on the pesticide efficacy estimates included in these guides

Insecticide and fungicide efficacy estimates were calculated mainly from trial results published in Arthropod Management Tests (published by the Entomological Society of America) and Plant Disease Management Reports (published by the American Phytopathological Society). Some pesticides allowed for organic production have been tested in many trials; others very few. Our goal was to present objective estimates by averaging the percent improvement provided by a given active ingredient compared with an untreated control, and to indicate how many trials were included in the calculation. We also indicate how many of the results included in the calculation were different (as determined by a statistical analysis) from the untreated control. When compiling a collection of trial results there is often a wide range of levels of improvement for a given pesticide/pest combination because of different rates of application, pest pressure, weather conditions, and a variety of other factors. The estimates provided here should not be considered a guarantee that a given pest reduction can be expected.
